title: Five post-acute settings, one register, ratios of 1.15x to 31.55x
excerpt: Medicare publishes the statutory price and the provider count for five post-acute settings. Set each published market size against that register and the ratio runs from 1.15x to 31.55x.
author: NeoGraph Analytics Research Desk
content:
Medicare pays for post-acute care in five settings. For each one it publishes the price by law, in the Federal Register, every year; for each one it publishes how many certified providers exist; and for each one its own advisory commission publishes what the program actually spent. Five markets, five statutory prices, five federal headcounts. If market sizing is ever checkable, it is checkable here.

We have now sized all five. Set each published headline against the Medicare register for the same setting and the ratios do not cluster anywhere:

SettingPublished headline, 2026Medicare FFS registerRatio
Home health$504.80B$16.0B31.55x
Skilled nursing$453.31B$31B14.62x
Long-term care hospitals$23.62B$2.4B9.84x
Inpatient rehabilitation$23.72B$11.62B2.04x
Hospice$32.60B$28.3B1.15x

The ratio runs from 1.15x to 31.55x across five settings of one program — a 27.4-fold difference in how far the published market departs from the same federal benefit. That spread is not a forecasting disagreement and it is not a data problem. Every denominator above is measured and every price above is statutory. It is one thing only: how much of each setting's name has been annexed by services the program does not pay for.

Hospice is the control

Hospice is where the published market and the register nearly meet, and the reason is structural rather than editorial. Medicare is almost the entire payer. VITAS, the largest operator to disclose it, reports Medicare at 93.1% of its hospice revenue for 2025, up from 91.2% in 2024. When one payer is 93% of the sector, a house sizing "the hospice market" has almost nothing else to count, so its headline lands within 15% of the register whether it set out to or not.

That makes hospice the control case for every other row. It establishes that the sizing houses are capable of landing on the register — that a 1.15x result is achievable — which removes the charitable reading of the 31.55x result. The gap elsewhere is not incapacity.

Hospice does carry its own striking failure, but it is a failure of labelling rather than of level: on a 2026 base its published estimates spread 25.4x, from $5.93B to $150.40B, and both of those figures are published by the same house in two different reports. One publisher, one base year, 25x apart. Our hospice report names the four tiers that spread resolves into.

Home health is the annexation case, and the publishers say so themselves

At the other end, home health's 31.55x needs no speculation about scope, because the houses print their scope. Coherent's definition covers "unskilled home healthcare" alongside blood sugar monitors, mobility aids, blood pressure monitors and pregnancy test kits. Persistence includes pregnancy care. Grand View splits its market into Equipment and Services and puts services at only 83.9% of 2025 revenue, which means roughly a sixth of its "home health care market" is hardware.

None of that is in the Medicare home health benefit, which pays a $2,038.22 national 30-day period rate — set, as it happens, on the calendar year, unlike the other four settings, all of which run on the federal fiscal year. So the 31.55x is not two houses disagreeing. It is a term of art in payment policy being used as the title of a much larger consumer and device market, and the two answers differing by thirty-one times.

The register confirms it is the numerator that moved, not the denominator: $16.0B over 8.3 million 30-day periods is $1,927.71 per period, 0.9458 of the statutory rate, and $16.0B over 65.4 million visits is $244.65 against MedPAC's own published $245. The federal side reconciles to within a rounding error of itself.

What one house's own regional share does to its own headline

There is a sharper test available here than the usual one, and three of these five markets fail it. A global house that publishes a North America share has handed over a bridge between its global total and a federal measurement, and the bridge can be walked.

Take the share, apply it to the house's own headline, and compare the result against what the United States alone had already measurably spent — advanced, if you like, at the house's own growth rate. North America contains the United States, so the implied region cannot be the smaller number.

In skilled nursing, Coherent publishes North America at 45.3% for 2026. That is 0.453 × $453.31B = $205.35B, which is 6.62% below the $219.9B the CMS national accounts measured for the United States alone in 2024, two years earlier, in a series that rose 7.3% that year. At Coherent's own 9.3%, the 2024 actual reaches $262.70B by 2026, which forces North America to at least 57.95% of its published total — or forces the total itself to $262.70B / 0.453 = $579.92B, 1.28x what is printed. One of the two numbers on that page is wrong, and nothing public says which.

In home health the same test fails twice more. Coherent's North America comes out 3.80% below the measured United States alone; Fortune's comes out 8.42% below — and Fortune's is not even a share we had to multiply out, because it publishes North America as a dollar figure, $172.64B for 2025. Grand View passes, with North America 9.67% above the US alone and $18.09B left for the rest of the world, which is why it is the series we publish.

This is worth stating plainly: the test is not hard, and it is not obscure. It needs one published share, one published headline, and one number from the national health accounts. Three of five houses examined here fail it on their own two numbers.

The setting with no published size at all

Inpatient rehabilitation is the one we could not source, and the absence is the finding. Across roughly twenty houses we found reports titled to "medical rehabilitation services", "rehabilitation" and "post-acute care"; two of them name the inpatient rehabilitation facility as a segment and publish a growth rate for it while withholding its size. Not one publishes a dollar figure for the IRF.

That absence sits on top of the best-measured setting of the five. The FY2026 rule reconciles to the cent: $18,907 × 1.026 × 1.0001 × 0.9985 = $19,371, and multiplying that standard amount by the published case-mix weights reproduces the published payment rates exactly — 19,371 × 0.7244 = $14,032.35 at the bottom of the 94-group table and 19,371 × 4.5328 = $87,804.87 at the top. A statutory price, 94 case-mix weights, a facility census split by ownership, claims-derived stays, occupancy and margin. And no published market size.

So we built one, from MedPAC and the Federal Register, and we say on the report in five places that it is a construction rather than a citation, with both derivation routes printed and their 3.94% divergence stated. A labelled construction from federal measurements is worth more than a citation to a house that never measured the thing. It is still the only headline in this corpus that is ours rather than a publisher's, and it is labelled as such everywhere it appears.

The pattern, and where it stops being about scope

Sort the five by ratio and the order is almost exactly the order of how much non-Medicare activity shares each setting's name. Hospice, at 1.15x, has essentially none. Inpatient rehabilitation, at 2.04x, has a defined inpatient facility and little else that can borrow the term. Long-term care hospitals, at 9.84x, are confused with "long term care" generally — we found houses sizing nursing homes and assisted living under the LTCH name at 474x the register. Skilled nursing, at 14.62x, is read as institutional long-term care worldwide. Home health, at 31.55x, has been annexed outright.

Two of the five, though, break the pattern we had been reporting, and they are worth separating. In clinical laboratory services and in home health, the growth estimates disagree more than the size estimates do — 1.97x against 1.480x, and 1.579x against 1.344x. Where that inversion appears, naming the scope fixes nothing, because the publishers already agree what the market is. What they are disagreeing about is a statutory rate path: PAMA's laboratory fee cuts, blocked on 3 February 2026 but still authorised for 2027 through 2029, and the calendar-2026 home health rate. The forecast is a forecast of policy, and it is being sold as a forecast of demand.

What to do with a post-acute number

Ask which of three things it is before anything else. The Medicare benefit — a statutory per-diem, per-period or per-stay amount times a federal volume, which is knowable to within a rounding error. The all-payer United States sector, which adds Medicaid and private pay and roughly triples the smaller settings. Or a global institutional category that keeps the setting's name and counts equipment, unskilled care and adjacent services inside it.

Added together, the five published headlines come to $1,038.05B against $89.3B of Medicare register across the five chapters — 11.62x, on figures whose years differ by setting and which we would not defend as a single estimate of anything. We print it only to make the scale of the gap concrete. Every ratio in this article divides a published figure by a federal one, and every one is reproducible from the two numbers named beside it. That is the whole method, and it is available to anyone who reads a rule and a MedPAC chapter before quoting a headline.
